messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Vega, a 59-year-old divorced physical therapist, described growing up in a home where a caregiver’s violence was ordinary enough to feel both unforgettable and somehow unreal. As a child, she was hit, shoved, and cornered in ways that taught her to stay small and constantly alert, but when she tries to picture those years now, the memories do not settle into a clear story. She can recall specific moments in fragments—a hand raised over a kitchen sink, the sting of fear in a hallway, the smell of bleach—then the images vanish as quickly as they came. At other times she can speak of what happened with a flat, distant numbness, as if she were describing abuse that happened to someone else. What unsettled her most was that the abuse felt so extreme, so outside what she later understood as normal family life, that it has often seemed hard for her to believe it truly happened to her at all.

Those broken memories have long shaped how Marisol moves through the world. Because the past can surface without warning, she has come to avoid anything that might stir it up: difficult conversations, family gatherings, crowded places, anything unpredictable or stressful. She keeps her apartment meticulously ordered, cleaning and reorganizing again and again because the physical routine gives her a sense of control when her mind does not. She also finds herself eating far more than she needs, especially in the evening, using food to blunt distress that otherwise feels hard to contain. Her work as a physical therapist has become a carefully managed environment; she can function, but she chooses the most familiar routines and tries to limit situations that feel emotionally taxing. In practice, that means she often turns down extra responsibilities and leaves herself little margin for anything that could upset the balance she has built.

Marisol’s sense of danger is not vague. In ordinary situations she feels threatened by strangers who approach too quickly, and in waiting rooms, store aisles, or the clinic lobby she will quietly angle herself so her back is against a wall and she can see the room. When she rides the elevator at work or hears footsteps behind her in a corridor, her body responds as if something bad is about to happen. At night she wakes and checks whether she is safe, scanning the apartment before she can settle back down. Those moments of threat have a way of pulling the past forward: if a man in the parking lot comes too close, or if someone raises a voice unexpectedly, a fragment of childhood can flash into mind and then disappear, leaving behind the same cold certainty she knew as a girl. In that sense, the danger she feels in the present feeds the brokenness of the memory, and the memory in turn makes ordinary contact with strangers feel even less safe.

Over the years, Marisol has organized her life around the hope that if she stays controlled enough, nothing will break through. She cleans, avoids stress, and keeps herself busy, but the relief never lasts. The more she tries to keep distress out, the more keyed up she becomes, watching doors, watching faces, watching for movement near her shoulders. That constant guarding makes it harder for her memories to hold together; they come as flashes, detached and unreal, just enough to remind her what she is trying not to feel. Then the numbness and the uncertainty push her back toward more control, more cleaning, more avoidance, and more overeating at night when she feels depleted. Her eating, in turn, is followed by the same disappointed, heavy sense that she has not really escaped anything.

Recently, the pattern began to interfere more noticeably with her work and daily life. She found herself declining lunch with colleagues, avoiding staff gatherings, and choosing routes through the clinic that let her keep a wall at her back. Even in her own apartment she became more restless at night, waking to check locks and windows, and then lying awake with old fragments drifting in and out of awareness. The accumulation of this has left Marisol feeling worn down and ashamed, especially because she has always prided herself on helping other people regain function. She finally sought help after realizing that her routines were no longer just habits but the limits of her life. What frightens her most is that the past may keep invading her present in pieces she cannot control, and what she most hopes for is to feel safe enough to rest without constantly bracing for the next threat.
